topics.title: Nine Cells: a merge tower defense game (testnet)

recent_posts.topic_title: Nine Cells: a merge tower defense game (testnet)
recent_posts.author: karasbuilder
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone, I’m Karas, a CKBuilder in the current cohort. I’ve been building Nine Cells, a browser tower defense game where you defend a wall by placing cats in lanes and merging two same-level cats into a stronger one. I’d like to share how it uses cells and get feedback, both on the game and on the script design.
Play it: https://nine-cells.karasdev.com/ (CKB testnet)
You can play the battles without a wallet. A CKB testnet wallet (JoyID or UTXO Global) is only needed to mint and keep cats on chain. Testnet CKB from the faucet covers the capacity and fees.
Why cells fit this game
The core action in the game is “two cats in, one stronger cat out”. That is exactly what a CKB transaction does: consume input cells, create output cells. So I didn’t need a contract with balances or a registry. Each cat you own is just a cell under your lock, and the rules live in one type script that checks every transaction touching those cells.
A CatCell is a cell with 8 bytes of data:
Byte
Field
0
version
1
level (1 to 255)
2
line / skin (1 to 21, 0 = unopened crate)
3
role (0 to 3)
4 to 7
block number at mint (metadata only)
The capacity locked in the cell (about 134 CKB at the moment) goes back to the owner when a cat is released.
One type script, dispatched by transaction shape
The script is written in TypeScript and runs on ckb-js-vm. It doesn’t read an “action” flag from the witness. It looks at how many cells of its own type are in the inputs and outputs, so a transaction can’t claim to be one action while doing another:
Inputs
Outputs
Action
What the script checks
0
1 or more
Mint
Only unopened crates at a fixed level (9). Nobody can mint a chosen cat directly.
n
n
Transfer / Reveal
Cat data must be unchanged (gift, batch move), or a crate becomes the cat picked by the seed below.
1 or more
0
Release
Burns the cat, capacity returns to the wallet.
2, 4 or 8
1
Merge
Same level and version; output level = input level + log2(count); output keeps the line of the last input.
Every rule has its own exit code, so a failing test points at the exact rule that broke. I checked the script against a real devnet node with 30 deliberately invalid transactions, and each was rejected with the expected code.
Random cats without an oracle
Opening a crate is a commit and reveal:
Mint creates an unopened crate cell.
Reveal spends the crate and creates the cat. The cat’s line must equal 1 + u32(seed) % 21, where seed = blake2b(nonce ‖ transactions_root ‖ crate outpoint) of the block right after the block that contains the crate. The transaction carries both headers in header_deps, and the script recomputes the seed.
When the crate is created, that next block doesn’t exist yet, so the player can’t predict or pick the result, and the script refuses any other line.
A known limit I’d like opinions on: a player can mint many crates, open them all, keep the line they want and release the rest for only the fees. Mint is open and fixed at level 9 on purpose (the client can’t prove a battle was won), so I’m unsure whether to treat this as acceptable or change the design.
What stays off chain, on purpose
Battles, placing cats, in-battle merges, stars, XP and gems all stay local in the browser. The battle runs on the client, so putting results on chain wouldn’t prove a fair game. I also looked at Spore DOBs and decided against them, because Spore content is immutable and a merge needs to rewrite the cat’s data.
The game has an optional fast mode: a session wallet you fund once, which then signs Vault actions without a popup and sweeps cats back to your main wallet. The trade-off is that its key lives in browser storage, so it’s for small amounts only.
Status on testnet
Type ID: 0xbc7cc190ac166a31de875e6fc4b0571903d62c665c25a84ec4f971277dd4126d
Latest upgrade (v4, 21 cat lines, 23 Oct): 0x700b17fb…609c6d
Earlier wallet-signed examples (v3.1): mint, reveal, four-cat merge, session wallet sweep

Byte Field
0 version

Inputs Outputs Action What the script checks
0 1 or more Mint Only unopened crates at a fixed level (9). Nobody can mint a chosen cat directly.
n n Transfer / Reveal Cat data must be unchanged (gift, batch move), or a crate becomes the cat picked by the seed below.
1 or more 0 Release Burns the cat, capacity returns to the wallet.
2, 4 or 8 1 Merge Same level and version; output level = input level + log2(count); output keeps the line of the last input.

  1. Mint creates an unopened crate cell.
  2. Reveal spends the crate and creates the cat. Battles, placing cats, in-battle merges, stars, XP and gems all stay local in the browser. The battle runs on the client, so putting results on chain wouldn’t prove a fair game. I also looked at Spore DOBs and decided against them, because Spore content is immutable and a merge needs to rewrite the cat’s data.

The game has an optional fast mode: a session wallet you fund once, which then signs Vault actions without a popup and sweeps cats back to your main wallet. The trade-off is that its key lives in browser storage, so it’s for small amounts only.

topics.title: [DIS] CKB IDL: Interface Description Language and Discoverability for CKB Scripts

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] CKB IDL: Interface Description Language and Discoverability for CKB Scripts
recent_posts.author: OWK50GA
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks for the thoughtful feedback, @3m1n3nc3
Developer experience is one of my biggest priorities here. The goal is to make IDL generation and consumption fit naturally into existing development workflows, rather than introduce another complicated process. That’s partly why I’m working on Molecule-to-IDL generation and TypeScript support.
On discoverability and composability, I agree. The Registry is intended to be a discovery and verification layer, not a source of trust. Consumers should be able to independently verify cryptographically bound interfaces against deployed scripts, regardless of where they retrieved the IDL.
Type Script support and richer transaction-level interfaces are directions I’d love to explore, but there is need to establish the initial lock-witness standard, and then extend the capability.
I’d like to be able to discover and integrate unfamiliar CKB scripts with as little script-specific knowledge as possible, while preserving independent verification, and I think other developers would too, hehe.

recent_posts.author: OWK50GA
recent_posts.content_text:
Thank you, Arthur. I really appreciate the support, and especially your help exploring IDL integration with the CellScript registry earlier.
I agree that the strongest approach is to complement existing tooling rather than duplicate it. CellScript’s existing type information makes IDL generation a particularly interesting integration, and I’d love to explore that further.
I am also exploring how IDL could complement SSRI, particularly where standardized interface descriptions and encoding could help external consumers.
There’s a lot to do, this is just the start

topics.title: [DIS] Kirea Finance: Native RWA Lending Infrastructure for CKB |【DIS】Kirea Finance：面向 CKB 的原生 RWA 借贷基础设施

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Kirea Finance: Native RWA Lending Infrastructure for CKB |【DIS】Kirea Finance：面向 CKB 的原生 RWA 借贷基础设施
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Interesting concept, and I appreciate the considerable development effort already invested in Kirea Finance. However, I still see a fundamental challenge with real-world asset (RWA) enforcement.
CKB can enforce on-chain contracts, but it cannot enforce real-world obligations.
What happens if an invoice is never paid? What if the borrower receives payment but never reports it? How can the system verify that an invoice is genuine, unpaid, and hasn’t already been pledged elsewhere?
Ultimately, this requires trusted third parties, external verification, and legal enforcement.
Who takes responsibility for verifying and enforcing the underlying asset, and who bears the loss if the debtor defaults?
I understand that these aspects are outside the current grant’s scope, but they seem essential to making RWA lending viable. Without them, the system risks becoming an on-chain representation of claims that cannot actually be enforced.
A possible alternative use case
Given the work already completed, perhaps Kirea Finance could be adapted to solve a more practical problem where the underlying funds are directly controlled by CKB.
One possibility would be milestone-based escrow and conditional payments for freelancers, contractors, or DAO grants.
For example:
A client deposits funds into a CKB smart contract.
The agreement and payment milestones are represented on-chain.
Funds are released progressively when authorized parties approve completed milestones.
Refunds, deadlines, and disputes follow predefined rules, potentially involving an agreed independent arbitrator.
This would still require some off-chain trust to confirm that work has been completed, but the funds themselves would be secured on-chain, and the approval mechanism would be explicit and transparent.
Much of the existing Kirea infrastructure could potentially be reused:
Asset Cells to represent agreements and milestones.
KYC/Attestation Cells to identify authorized participants or approvers.
Lending contract logic as a starting point for conditional payments, settlement, and refunds.
Rather than attempting to make real-world collateral enforceable through blockchain technology, this approach could focus on a problem that CKB can directly help solve: ensuring that committed funds are available and distributed according to agreed conditions.
Perhaps Kirea could evolve into a more general-purpose framework for conditional payments, escrow, and milestone-based agreements, with RWA lending remaining one possible future application.
I think this direction could preserve much of the valuable work already completed while offering a clearer path toward a practical use case within the Nervos ecosystem.

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Kirea Finance: Native RWA Lending Infrastructure for CKB |【DIS】Kirea Finance：面向 CKB 的原生 RWA 借贷基础设施
recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text:
Thanks @psawyerberlin for the thoughtful, detailed feedback and for recognizing the work already invested in Kirea Finance. You’ve raised two important points, and I appreciate both the critical questions about RWA enforcement and the constructive comment.
1. On RWA Enforcement & Verification
You’re right that blockchain code alone cannot verify an off-chain invoice, establish that it hasn’t already been pledged elsewhere, compel a real-world debtor to pay, or guarantee recovery following default.
Real-world collateral enforceability depends on complementary on-chain and off-chain components. Legal agreements, assignments, and appropriate recovery mechanisms establish the basis for pursuing a claim, while on-chain infrastructure enforce programmed rules, represent assets, and record state transitions. It’s a a two-piece puzzle" (on-chain rails + off-chain legal framework). Neither can work or replace the other.
This grant focuses on delivering that foundational technical layer: standardized compliant identity primitives (issuer-controlled KYC attestations), unique asset primitives, and hardened lending state machines. Establishing a compliant ID mechanism on-chain is the necessary first step toward legal ownership and real-world enforcement, providing a secure, auditable on-chain foundation that off-chain legal contracts and issuers can anchor to.
To address your point on risk and verification: making real-world collateral legally enforceable requires active integration between on-chain state and off-chain law, and I am building with that full lifecycle in mind. Beyond the smart contracts, this work directly enables real-world enforceability by providing standardized legal-to-code mapping, identity attestation structures, and operational documentation for Asset Issuers and SPVs to attach legal assignments, invoice verification processes, and recourse reserves directly to on-chain asset cells. I have updated Sections 3.4 and 10 to clearly detail how this grant establishes both the technical rails and the operational blueprints necessary for real-world legal enforcement.
2. On Your Escrow & Milestone-Based Payment Suggestion
I think your escrow suggestion is a valuable direction to explore. It highlights how foundational CKB primitives could support applications beyond invoice financing, including milestone-based payments, contractor agreements, and DAO grant distribution.
There is potential to reuse parts of the architecture:
Milestone Escrow & DAO Grants: Asset Cells could represent agreements or milestones, while attestation mechanisms could identify authorized participants or approvers. Conditional releases, refunds, deadlines, and dispute handling would simply build on top of this contract logic.
Other Asset-Linked Applications: The same foundational approach could support representations of claims involving commodities, physical assets like gold, real estate, or equipment, provided the necessary asset verification and legal arrangements are established off-chain.
Summary
The goal of Phase 1 is to deliver a focused set of reusable, open-source CKB primitives (including compliant identity gating and asset state machines) that currently do not exist in the Nervos ecosystem. These components provide immediate value to future RWA deployments and DeFi development, while offering a foundation other builders may adapt for applications such as conditional payments and escrow.
Thank you again for raising these ideas. This is exactly the kind of constructive dialogue that strengthens ecosystem standards!

recent_posts.author: SalmanDev
recent_posts.content_text:
To address your point on risk and verification: Across the broader Web3 ecosystem (such as Centrifuge, Goldfinch, and Maple), no RWA protocol enforces real-world obligations through smart contracts alone. They rely on the two complementary layers working together: off-chain legal SPVs and court jurisdictions handle invoice verification and default enforcement, while on-chain smart contracts enforce asset state transitions, identity gating, and liquidity rules.
This grant brings that exact industry-standard architecture to Nervos by delivering the missing on-chain foundation, compliant identity primitives, asset cells, and state machines along with legal-to-code mapping documentation. I have updated Sections 3.4 and 10 on metaforo to explicitly include the operational separation between technical rails and off-chain enforcement.
This is foundational infrastructure that must be built if CKB is to support scalable RWA protocols.

topics.title: Cellula Wallet beta on testnet: testers wanted until Monday 26 October

recent_posts.topic_title: Cellula Wallet beta on testnet: testers wanted until Monday 26 October
recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
image1920×1008 241 KB
Hi everyone,
Cellula is the name you can pay: cellula.id gives you one name, yourname.cell, that people can pay instead of a blockchain address. Now we are testing the Cellula Wallet, a wallet that lives in your passkey, and we are looking for more testers: on Android, where the app is, and on the web, where the same wallet runs in any browser that can save a passkey. The beta runs until Monday 26 October at midnight (23:59 UTC).
What it is
Your passkey is the wallet: you open it with your fingerprint, face or screen lock, and there is no seed phrase to write down.
An Android app (Android 11 or later), and the same wallet on the web.
.cell names right in the wallet: pay a name, and be paid at yours.
A Fiber balance for instant payments, through Cellula’s Fiber node. Its keys stay on your device.
Savings in the Nervos DAO, and a Quantum Vault locked with a signature built to resist quantum computers.
Private payments to your name, tokens and DOBs, and guardians who can help you get the wallet back if you lose your passkey.
Sites can connect to it, ask it to sign, sign in with a .cell name, and take Fiber payments.
Everything runs on the testnet with test coins, so nothing you do costs real money.
How the beta works
Testers get a step by step test plan: twelve basic tests anyone can do, in the app or in a browser, and advanced ones for those who want to go deeper. Reports go to a private testers’ group, one problem per message, and we ship fixes from them as they come in. The first round from our testers’ reports went live within a day.
How to join
Join our Telegram at Telegram: View @cellula_id and tell us how you will test: on Android (your phone model and Android version) or in a browser (which one). We add testers to the group in small batches, so the test network stays usable for everyone. The basic tests take about an hour, so there is still time: the beta closes on Monday 26 October at midnight (23:59 UTC).
Thanks, and see you there.

recent_posts.content_text:
GM NERVOS BUILDERS!!!,
The product previously called Mint Gate is now Nervlith (formally Mint Gate).
Nervlith is a CKB-native DAO launcher, token gating and membership platform.
image1775×748 141 KB
It is also translated to Mandarin for wider community scope
image1375×677 103 KB
How Does Nervlith work
Nervlith works in a simple way:
Own a DID passport, without an identity on Nervlith you can’t access or join communities.
image1728×808 65.3 KB
image752×811 47.2 KB
Create a community, choose a governance model, add a gate fee, Membership Card design.
image980×789 46.5 KB
image1061×824 61.2 KB
image1115×806 111 KB
image832×746 72.3 KB
Join a community created by someone by paying the gate fee.
Get an xUDT (NFT) membership card that gives you access to the community.
image1116×747 73.2 KB
Participate in community activities e.g. voting on proposals.
It is that simple.
Demo: https://nervlith.vercel.app/
Repository: GitHub - Victor-Okenwa/nervlith: A CKB-native token-gating/membership platform for governance, proposals and community management · GitHub
Network: CKB testnet
The Problem
A hosted forum keeps membership in an operator’s database, proposals in a chat room, and identity in a handle that stays with the host. The chain never sees who belonged, who paid, or which model the community chose.
CKB already has the pieces for a community the VM can check: a cell for the community, a type script for its rules, xUDT for membership, and DID:CKB for a passport that travels with the person. Nervlith is the launcher that puts those pieces in one place.
What Nervlith is
A community is a gate fee plus a governance model.
Build. The founder launches the community as cells. They set a name, a description, a gate fee of at least 200 CKB, and a governance model. The community type script checks those fields on creation and stores the chosen model on the community cell, so later governance can read it from the same schema.
Govern. Paying the fee mints a membership. When voting arrives, each vote is its own intent cell. A tally reads those cells and updates community state. The voter signs the vote once. The tally does the rest.
Belong. DID:CKB is the passport across communities. Nervlith keeps a single account system: that DID. The membership card is how belonging to one community looks.
Governance models
The community contract accepts three models. Any of the three may be stored on the community cell. The models mimics real world governing modes.
Autocracy (The North Korea)
The owner keeps control. Members hold a card, and the owner decides.
Democracy (The American Model)
Available once governance starts. One membership, one vote. Any member may propose. All members vote. The owner can be voted out.
Legislative (The English)
Available after that first voting trial has real communities behind it. Members elect a council. The council votes on laws between elections.
Democracy and Legislative follow AnihDev’s CKB voting pattern (which will be integrated into the project) into Nervlith. Each vote is an independent intent cell. Nervlith will build the transaction that creates the vote cell, and a separate aggregation flow will read those cells. Aggregation does not ask the voter to sign again. The ballots stay in their own cells.
The first governance trial is the basic one: a proposal, a vote, one card, one vote. Councils wait until communities are actually forming.
Projects Nervlith builds on
Nervlith is a launcher around cell-native work that is already on CKB.
CCC
Common Chains Connector is how Nervlith talks to the chain. Wallets, cells, and typed transaction builders go through CCC. Every transaction declares cellDeps for the scripts it uses. Where a script reads a witness, the Rust script and the TypeScript builder use the same slot.
DID:CKB and Vellum
Identity is DID:CKB through @ckb-ccc/did-ckb, with profile records from Vellum by truthixify. A person can create a DID, resolve it, edit the profile, rotate keys, deactivate it, and migrate from did:plc. That DID is the passport every community recognizes.
After governance, Vellum claims can attach to the same DID: a small cell issued by someone else, such as a verified GitHub handle or a completed CKB task. Those claims may later weight a vote or open a gate.
Intent-cell governance
AnihDev’s voting dapp is the pattern for Democracy and Legislative, linked above. Nervlith will implement that pattern in its own proposal cells, vote cells, and tally. The MVP does the launch and the gate first. The vote cells come with the governance phase.
The contracts are no_std Rust on ckb-std. The app is Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind.
What the MVP covers
The project could be large and so I have decided to cut down building time by focusing on the most important parts.
The MVP is three phases: identity, community creation, and a gate that checks membership. The owner keeps control through that span. Voting and other community activities is the phase after the MVP.
What you can use now
The demo at https://nervlith.vercel.app/ currently includes:
A DID on the connected wallet: create, resolve, edit the profile, rotate keys, deactivate, and migrate from did:plc.
A shell for the passport: landing, dashboard, browse communities, and My Identity.
A four-step launch: name and description, gate fee and model, a live card designer, and review.
A community type script that checks the name, the gate fee, and the governance model, and stores the model on the community cell.
The founder’s membership: an owner-mode xUDT of amount 1, and the card drawn from that community’s metadata.
Autocracy is the model a launch can select today.
What the MVP still includes
The join flow: pay the gate fee, mint the membership xUDT, and show the card.
A lock script that opens an action only when the transaction inputs include that community’s membership xUDT.
The same witness slot on both sides of that lock: input_type.
After the MVP
Democracy as the first voting trial, then Legislative council elections.
Proposal cells, independent vote cells, and an aggregation flow.
Reputation claims on the DID, after governance.
Try the demo
Open https://nervlith.vercel.app/.
Connect a wallet on CKB testnet.
Open My Identity and create a DID, or migrate a did:plc you already hold.
Launch a community. Set the name, a gate fee of at least 200 CKB, and Autocracy, then design the card.
Review the card. The launch mints that membership to the wallet that signs.
Use testnet CKB. A launch lands when the community script is deployed on the network you are connected to. The source is at GitHub - Victor-Okenwa/nervlith: A CKB-native token-gating/membership platform for governance, proposals and community management · GitHub .
Feedback
I would value notes from people building on CKB, especially on:
Whether a membership card backed by an owner-mode xUDT reads clearly as membership.
Whether Autocracy is the right model to run first, with Democracy and Legislative already stored on the community cell.
What you would put behind a card if the first communities are for CKB builders.
Thanks for reading. I look forward to the discussion.
